---
title: "Overview of the IRW Data Standards"
---

Data standards are an essential mechanism of increasing reusability and interoperability of data amongst researchers. As such, they play a critical role in increasing the extent to which science is [FAIR](https://www.nature.com/articles/sdata201618) (findable, accessible, interoperable, reusable). The IRW's response data come in several *data families* that use distinct data standards. We focus here on describing the families and the differences between their standards (with pointers to complete descriptions of the specific standards).

## The data families {#families}

Every response table in the IRW belongs to exactly one **data family**, and each family is kept in its own Redivis dataset. In the `irw` packages, the `source` argument selects the family.

| Family | `source =` | What defines it |
|---|---|---|
| Core | `"core"` (the default) | A person responds to an item; the responses are ordered or continuous |
| Nominal | `"nom"` | As in core, but the response categories have no order |
| Competitions | `"comp"` | Two agents meet and an outcome is recorded, including pairwise comparisons of fixed things such as essays |
| Simulated and synthetic | `"sim"` | Responses that no real person produced |
| Conjoint | `"conj"` | Respondents choose between, or rate, profiles whose attributes are assigned at random |

Four families are defined by the shape of the data. Simsyn is defined by where the data come from: a simulated table can have any shape, and it belongs to simsyn rather than to the family its shape would suggest. The line between competitions and conjoint is what gets compared. In competitions the same named entities meet again and again; in a conjoint experiment each profile is a new random bundle of attributes.

Item text and the metadata are not families. They hold no responses and describe the tables in the families.

## The data standards

In all cases, we are interested in cross-classified responses. The differences amongst the standards pertain to the nature of either the cross-classification or the response.
